title: the twin arjuna trees
hook: a boy drags his mortar between two old trees, and two cursed brothers step out free
carry: darshan: to see the Lord, and be seen

segments.voice: Yesterday every rope came up two fingers short, until Krishna let his tired mother tie him. Your line was love is the only rope that holds God.
screen: `THE BUTTER THIEF.` · `HE LETS HIMSELF BE TIED.`

segments.voice: So there he is, a small boy roped to a heavy wooden mortar, and his mother has gone back to her housework. A child might sulk, or cry. Krishna looks around the yard. Near the house stand two tall arjuna trees, side by side. And the Bhagavata lets us in on something nobody in the village knows: those two trees used to be people. They've been standing there a long time, waiting for this exact boy. Today the mortar goes for a walk.
screen: `TIED TO THE MORTAR.` → `TWO ARJUNA TREES.` → `THEY USED TO BE PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: The trees were once Nalakuvara and Manigriva, the sons of Kubera, the god of wealth. Proud and drunk, they were playing in a river with a crowd of young women, wearing nothing, when the sage Narada happened by. The women, embarrassed, covered themselves at once. The brothers didn't bother. So Narada cursed them to stand as trees, but his curse came with a way out: they would stand until they came before Krishna, and then be free. Now Krishna toddles toward them, dragging the mortar. He squeezes between the trunks. The mortar turns sideways and wedges against them. He pulls, and with a great crack both trees come crashing down. Out step two shining figures. They bow to the child, praise him, and ask that every part of them be his from now on: their words for his praise, their hands for his work, their eyes for seeing his holy ones. Then they go. The cowherds come running at the noise. The children playing nearby say: Krishna did it, dragging the mortar. The grown-ups can hardly believe it. Nanda unties his son, smiling. Here's the teaching. After ages as trees, what ended the curse was one thing: they came before him and saw him. Hindus call that seeing darshan. It's why people stand in long temple lines, especially at midnight on Janmashtami, for a few seconds before the deity. And in Hindu practice darshan goes both ways: you see the Lord, and the Lord sees you. One sight, and the brothers want even their eyes turned toward the holy from then on.
screen: `KUBERA'S SONS, PROUD AND DRUNK.` · `NARADA'S CURSE, WITH A WAY OUT.` · `THE MORTAR WEDGES BETWEEN THEM.` · then, large: `DARSHAN: TO SEE AND BE SEEN.`

segments.voice: If you have an image of Krishna, or of any deity, sit in front of it and simply look for a minute, without asking for anything: the eyes, the face, the hands. If you don't, look at something you find sacred, or at the sky. Let yourself be looked at, too. If you don't pray, just let the looking be slow and full.
Nalakuvara. One of two proud, drunk sons of Kubera, cursed to stand as trees until they saw Krishna and were set free.
Your line: darshan, to see the Lord and be seen. Tomorrow, a mother looks into a small mouth. That's a week, done.

screen: `DAY 889 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE MOUTH FULL OF UNIVERSE.`

howItsDone: The freeing of Kubera's sons, called Yamalarjuna in Sanskrit, the twin arjuna trees, is retold in Krishna devotion as part of the Damodara story, and some images show the child pulling the mortar between two trees.
